clinicalPearls: A smoking-related interstitial lung disease occurring almost exclusively in current or former heavy cigarette smokers, usually presenting in mid-adult life.
Represents the symptomatic, clinically significant end of the spectrum of respiratory bronchiolitis, a near-universal incidental finding in smokers.
Typically presents with insidious cough and mild exertional dyspnoea, with fine crackles on auscultation and, uncommonly, clubbing.
It lies on a pathological continuum with desquamative interstitial pneumonia, both being smoking-related and sharing pigmented macrophage accumulation.
High-resolution computed tomography shows centrilobular nodules, ground-glass opacities and bronchial wall thickening, often with upper-zone-predominant centrilobular emphysema.
Histology demonstrates pigmented (tan-brown) macrophages accumulating within respiratory bronchioles and surrounding alveoli with mild peribronchiolar inflammation and fibrosis.
Smoking cessation is the primary treatment and can produce stabilisation or improvement; corticosteroids are used selectively with variable benefit.
Lung function typically shows a mixed obstructive-restrictive pattern with a reduced gas transfer factor.
reference.pathophysiology: RB-ILD is driven by chronic exposure to cigarette smoke, which induces recruitment and activation of alveolar macrophages within and around the respiratory bronchioles. These macrophages accumulate finely granular golden-brown cytoplasmic pigment representing phagocytosed smoke-derived particulate material. The inhaled irritants provoke a low-grade inflammatory response in the terminal and respiratory bronchioles, with infiltration by lymphocytes and histiocytes, mild peribronchiolar fibrosis and extension of the process into adjacent alveolar ducts and alveoli. In respiratory bronchiolitis these changes are patchy and asymptomatic, but when the burden of macrophage accumulation and peribronchiolar inflammation is sufficient to impair gas exchange and cause symptoms, the disorder is designated RB-ILD. The condition overlaps mechanistically with desquamative interstitial pneumonia, in which the pigmented macrophage accumulation is more diffuse and alveolar-filling. Coexisting centrilobular emphysema and small-airway disease from the same smoking exposure contribute to the mixed physiological impairment. The dependence on tobacco exposure explains why disease often stabilises after cessation.
additionalDifferentials: Usual interstitial pneumonia / idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with small-airway disease
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution computed tomography of the thorax for centrilobular nodules and ground-glass change
Pulmonary function tests including gas transfer measurement
Bronchoalveolar lavage demonstrating pigmented smoker's macrophages
Surgical or transbronchial lung biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain
Exclusion of relevant occupational or environmental antigen exposures
Serology to help exclude connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease
redFlags: Progressive dyspnoea or falling gas transfer despite smoking cessation
Imaging features suggesting established fibrosis or honeycombing, pointing to an alternative diagnosis
Clinical or radiological features atypical for a smoking-related process
Development of pulmonary hypertension or cor pulmonale
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally favourable compared with fibrotic interstitial lung diseases; many patients stabilise or improve with smoking cessation, although some experience persistent symptoms or slow progression, and continued smoking is associated with worse outcomes.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosing RB-ILD from incidental respiratory bronchiolitis in an asymptomatic smoker without clinical and physiological correlation.
Failing to make smoking cessation the central intervention and relying on corticosteroids instead.
Confusing the imaging with hypersensitivity pneumonitis and missing a relevant antigen exposure.
Not recognising coexisting emphysema, which alters the physiological interpretation.
Mistaking the ground-glass changes for a fibrotic interstitial pneumonia and giving an unduly poor prognosis.
references: Fishman's Pulmonary Diseases and Disorders (standard reference)
management: Make smoking cessation the cornerstone of treatment with combined pharmacological and behavioural support, as it drives the disease and many patients stabilise or improve
Consider a trial of corticosteroids for persistent or progressive symptoms despite cessation, recognising the limited evidence base
Offer pulmonary rehabilitation and influenza and pneumococcal vaccination as supportive measures
Provide supplemental oxygen if significant hypoxaemia develops
Monitor symptoms, pulmonary function with gas transfer, and interval HRCT for progression
Manage within a specialist interstitial lung disease multidisciplinary team and reassess the diagnosis if progression is atypical
